title: The Sovereign Hardened Protocol (SHP): A Bare-Metal Architecture for Critical Healthcare Infrastructure Security and Resilient Communications
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Problem Statement: Critical infrastructures—including hospitals, pharmaceutical warehouses, and medical supply chains—face escalating threats ranging from cyberattacks and the theft of sensitive genomic and medical data to communication blackouts during crises. Proposed Solution: The Sovereign Hardened Protocol (SHP) is a military-grade, immutable bare-metal operating and communication system. It securely interconnects central cores, peripheral facilities, and emergency vehicles (ambulances) with uncompromising security and near-total operational continuity. Key Technical & Strategic Advantages: • Absolute Data Sovereignty: Utilizing Zero-Knowledge encryption and real-time in-memory (RAM) processing, the system ensures data remains the sole property of the institution, preventing unauthorized surveillance even from the central server itself. • Uninterrupted Transcontinental Connectivity: Intelligently integrates 5G networks, satellite communications, and radio frequencies (RF), reinforced by atomic-clock-synchronized frequency hopping to completely neutralize jamming and wireless interception. • Instant Cryptographic Shredding & Isolated Self-Recovery: Combines artificial intelligence with physical sensors to accurately detect genuine intrusions, executing immediate cryptographic key erasure to protect data without damaging hardware, followed by automated self-reconstruction within minutes from isolated backups secured via unidirectional Data Diodes with zero downtime. Intellectual Property & Scope: This technical note serves as an official timestamped conceptual overview of the SHP architecture. Underlying source codes, cryptographic implementations, and hardware integration schematics remain proprietary and confidential intellectual property.

title: Scoping Review on Decision-Making Processes in Hospitals During Meteorological Disasters
abstract: This project is a scoping review that aims to identify and map existing knowledge regarding how hospitals make initial disaster response decisions—particularly the activation of disaster management headquarters and staff mobilization—during meteorological disasters such as floods, typhoons, and hurricanes. The review follows the methodological framework of Arksey and O’Malley (2005) and adheres to the PRISMA-ScR and JBI guidelines. The objectives are: To identify decision-making triggers and processes for activating hospital disaster headquarters during meteorological disasters. To clarify how staff mobilization decisions are made and supported. To compare the use and applicability of decision-support tools such as timelines, checklists, and the Incident Command System (ICS) across different countries. The findings will contribute to developing a framework for hospital disaster preparedness in Japan.
